design-01.title: Visual Hierarchy
explain: When people first look at a screen or a sheet of paper, they do not read everything at once. The eye starts at the **most noticeable spot** and moves to the next most noticeable one. Designing this order is **visual hierarchy**.

There are four main tools for creating hierarchy.
- **Size**: the larger an element, the sooner it is read.
- **Weight**: even at the same size, bold type is seen first.
- **Contrast**: the greater the difference in color or brightness from the background, the more an element stands out.
- **Whitespace**: empty space around an element separates it and makes it stand out.
The key is **difference**. If everything is made large and bold, nothing stands out. Hierarchy means deciding “what matters more” and then giving differences in that order.

examples.title: Reading a poster

body.alt: Poster for a summer concert, titled “여름 음악회” (Summer Concert). The title is large, bold black text; the date and time are in green; the venue and contact are small grey text. The elements are arranged from top to bottom.

body: The title is the largest and boldest black text. The date and time are smaller than the title but set in green, which gives them contrast with the background. The venue and contact are small and pale grey, so they are read last.
The reading order is title → date and time → venue → contact. Size, weight and color each play a different role in this order.

design-02.title: Proximity and Grouping
explain: The eye sees things that are close together as a **single group**. It does this without being told to. This tendency is called **proximity**.

There are several ways to create groups.
- **Proximity**: things placed close together are grouped.
- **Similarity**: things that look alike in shape, color or size are grouped.
- **Alignment**: things placed on the same line are grouped.

So information that is related should be placed **close together**, and information that is unrelated should be placed **far apart**. If all the gaps are equal, it is impossible to tell which items belong together.
Groups can be formed with spacing alone, without lines or boxes. Removing lines and relying on spacing makes a screen lighter.

body: There are twelve dots, and their shape and color are the same. Yet they do not look like one line. They appear as **three groups of four**, because the gaps within each group are much narrower than the gaps between groups.

examples.title: Proximity on a business card

design-03.title: Grids and Alignment
explain: A **grid** is an invisible frame that divides the screen into regular columns. When elements are placed on the lines of the grid, they become **aligned** and give an orderly impression.

There are three kinds of grid elements.
- **Column**: the area into which an element fits. An element occupies one column or several.
- **Gutter**: the constant gap between columns.
- **Margin**: the edge outside the grid.

The basic principle of alignment is to **share a line**. When the left edges of different elements lie on the same vertical line, the eye follows that line. If the lines are even slightly off, the layout looks disorganized.

design-04.title: Three Properties of Color and Lightness Contrast
explain:
Color is described by three attributes.
- **Hue**: the name that distinguishes one color from another, such as red, blue or green.
- **Lightness**: how light or dark a color is. The closer it is to white, the higher its lightness; the closer to black, the lower.
- **Chroma**: how vivid or clear a color is. The more gray is mixed in, the lower the chroma and the duller the color.

The factor that matters most for reading text is not hue but **lightness contrast** (the difference in brightness). Green text on a red background differs entirely in hue, but the two are similar in brightness, so the text is hard to read. Dark backgrounds are easier to read with light text, and light backgrounds with dark text.

The principle that **color alone should not carry meaning** is also important. People differ in how well they distinguish colors, and screens are sometimes printed in black and white or viewed in strong sunlight. When signaling a status, use an **icon (shape) or a text label** together with color.

body: Box 가 has a large difference in brightness between text and background, so it can be read even from a distance. Box 나 has similar brightness, so it must be squinted at to be seen.

The two status indicators at the bottom use not only the green and orange colors but also a round check and a triangular exclamation **shape**, plus the words “정상 작동” and “점검 필요” as **text**. So they still convey their meaning in black and white.

design-05.title: Working with Type and Readable Lines
explain: Arranging text so that it is easy to read and understand is called **typography**. Before choosing a beautiful typeface, you adjust three numbers that keep the eye from losing its place in the lines.

- **Type size**: distinguishes body text from headings, creating a hierarchy.
- **Line length**: the number of characters in a line. If a line is too long, the eye loses the start of the next line while searching for it; if it is too short, the eye must keep jumping to new lines, which causes fatigue.
- **Leading** (line spacing): the distance between the line above and the line below. If leading is too tight, the letters of adjacent lines seem to collide; if it is too loose, a paragraph looks scattered.

The key principle is that **leading should be wider than the spacing between words, but narrower than the spacing between paragraphs**. This applies the **proximity** principle from Lesson 2 to text itself.

design-06.title: Affordances and Feedback
explain: If posters only had to be read, screens on websites and devices are things people **operate**. A good screen shows how it should be handled, so that the user does not need a manual.

A clue in appearance that shows what an object can be used for is called an **affordance**. A handle is shaped to be pulled, and a button with a border and background color is shaped to be pressed. Conversely, if a pressable button is made to look exactly like ordinary body text, no one will know to press it.

When a person presses a button, the screen must immediately show that the action was accepted. This is **feedback**. The button changes color, or a message such as “신청 완료됨” (application completed) appears, so the user feels reassured that the press worked. Without feedback, users think the screen is broken and press the same button several times.

examples.title: The button's cue and response

body.alt: Three stages compared. A shows a plain piece of text, “예약 신청하기” (Book now), with no background or border. B shows the same words in white inside a rounded dark green box, which looks like a button. C shows the button turned grey with a check mark and the words “신청 완료됨” (application completed).
body.caption: A: no cue / B: affordance cue / C: feedback after the action

body: A looks like an ordinary heading or body text, so it is hard to tell that it can be pressed. B shows through its distinct box shape and contrast that it is a button (affordance). When the shape and label change after pressing, as in C, the user does not press again (feedback).

design-07.title: Type Anatomy and Font Classification
explain: In Lesson 5 you learned how to adjust type size, line length and leading. Yet it is common for two fonts set at the same 16px to look different in size: one looks large and the other small. Why do the numbers match but the sizes differ? To answer this, you need the names of the parts that make up a letter and of the guide lines used to measure them. This is **type anatomy**.

Latin lowercase letters are designed on four horizontal guide lines. The **baseline** is the line on which letters sit. The **x-height** is the height from the baseline to the top of the lowercase x. Strokes that rise above the x-height, such as in h, d or b, are called **ascenders**; strokes that descend below the baseline, such as in p, g or y, are called **descenders**. The height of capital letters is called the **cap height**. The important point is that the “type size” we specify is not the visible height of a letter. It is measured against the full body of the type, which includes the ascenders and descenders.

Therefore, at the same type size $s$, the x-height ratio $r$ differs from font to font. The visible lowercase height is $$h_x = r \times s$$ 이다. 본문은 대부분 소문자로 이루어지므로 $r$이 큰 글꼴이 같은 크기에서 더 커 보이고, 작은 크기에서도 잘 읽힌다. 두 글꼴의 보이는 크기를 맞추려면 $r_A s_A = r_B s_B$가 되도록 크기를 바꾸면 된다. (In English: Because body text is mostly lowercase, a font with a larger r looks larger at the same size and remains readable at small sizes. To match the visible sizes of two fonts, change their sizes so that r_A s_A = r_B s_B.)

explain.alt: Letters h, x and p drawn on four horizontal guide lines. From top to bottom the lines are labeled “어센더 선” (ascender line), “엑스하이트 선” (x-height line), “기준선” (baseline) and “디센더 선” (descender line). Only the baseline is a solid orange line. The vertical stroke of h rises to the top line, x sits between the second and third lines, and the stem of p descends to the bottom line.

explain: Read the figure. The vertical stroke of h rises to the top ascender line, x fills the space between the x-height line and the baseline, and the stroke of p descends to the descender line. Only the baseline is drawn as a solid line, because the letters in a single line must all share this line to look orderly.

Typefaces are broadly divided by the appearance of their strokes.
- **Serif**: small projections (serifs) at the ends of strokes. Often has contrast between thick and thin strokes.
- **Sans-serif**: no serifs; stroke weight is relatively even.
- **Monospaced**: all characters have the same width. Used for aligning numbers in code and tables.
- **Handwritten and display faces**: used for headings and short phrases.
In Korean, the **myeongjo (바탕) family**, with brush-like terminals, and the **gothic (돋움) family**, without them, correspond to this distinction. Because Hangul syllables are composed of initial, medial and final jamo, many typefaces fit each character into a square box, while some let the height vary with the presence of a final consonant rather than staying inside the square.

There are limits. The x-height ratio is not always listed in font specifications, and it looks slightly different depending on screen rendering, so it should be treated as an approximation. The boundaries of font classification are also blurred: many fonts, such as a serif with a very small serif or a sans-serif with strong stroke contrast, are hard to place cleanly in one category. Classification is not a way to pick the correct answer, but a starting point for comparing the character of fonts.

examples.title: Matching the visible sizes of two fonts
body: Condition: Body font A is 16px with an x-height ratio of 0.53. The font B to be used alongside it has a ratio of 0.45.
Step 1: The visible lowercase height of A is 16 × 0.53 = 8.48px. If B is also set at 16px, its lowercase height is 16 × 0.45 = 7.2px, which is noticeably smaller.
Step 2: Raising B's size to 8.48 ÷ 0.45 ≈ 18.8px makes the lowercase heights of the two fonts equal.
Interpretation: When mixing two fonts within one paragraph (for example, code inside body text), matching the x-height looks less awkward than matching the type-size numbers.

examples.title: Pairing heading and body fonts
body: Condition: In a hypothetical neighborhood newsletter, choose one font for the headings and one for the body text.
Step 1: Use a serif with pronounced stroke contrast for the heading, and an even-stroked sans-serif for the body. Begin by making them differ in classification.
Step 2: If both fonts are sans-serif and differ only slightly in shape, the mix looks like an accidental mistake. If you want a difference, make it clear through classification or weight.
Interpretation: The hierarchy principle from Lesson 1 (differences must be clear for an order to exist) applies to font selection as well.

design-08.title: Leading, Tracking and Line Length as Readability Numbers
explain: Sometimes text reads stuffily even when a good typeface has been chosen. Lines sit too close together, a line stretches all the way across the screen, or the spacing between letters is uneven. In Lesson 5 these problems were handled as principles. This lesson converts them into the **numbers** designers actually adjust.

First, distinguish two senses of “readability.” The ease with which each letter is told apart from the others (legibility) is determined mainly by the shape of the typeface. The ease with which a reader can keep going through long text (readability) depends largely on **layout numbers** such as leading, tracking and line length. This lesson deals with the latter.

**Leading** is usually set as a multiple of the type size. $$L = k \times s$$ 여기서 $s$는 글자 크기, $k$는 배수, $L$은 한 줄이 차지하는 높이다. 본문에는 대체로 1.4~1.6배 안팎이 많이 쓰이고, 줄이 길수록 다음 줄의 첫머리를 찾기 쉽도록 배수를 조금 넓힌다. 웹 접근성 지침(WCAG)에는 사용자가 줄 높이를 글자 크기의 1.5배, 문단 간격을 2배로 늘려도 내용이 잘리거나 겹치지 않아야 한다는 기준도 있다. (In English: Here s is the type size, k the multiplier and L the height taken up by one line. For body text, multipliers of about 1.4 to 1.6 are common, and the multiplier is widened slightly as the line gets longer, to make it easier to find the start of the next line. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) include a criterion that content must not be cut off or overlap when users increase line height to 1.5 times the type size and paragraph spacing to 2 times.)

**Tracking** (letter-spacing) is the value that widens or narrows the spacing between all letters, usually measured in units of 1/1000 of the type size (em). The actual change in spacing is $$\Delta = s \times \frac{t}{1000}$$ For example, applying tracking of +50 to 20px text separates each letter by 1px. For a short phrase set entirely in capitals, slightly wider tracking makes it easier to read, while very large headings often look wider than they are and are frequently tightened a little. Adjusting the spacing of one particular pair of letters (for example, A and V) is called **kerning** and is distinguished from tracking.

**Line length** is the number of characters per line. For Latin-script body text, a commonly cited rule of thumb is that about 45 to 75 characters per line is comfortable to read. If the line is too long, the eye loses the next line; if it is too short, frequent line breaks break the rhythm. These numbers together form a single order. As with the rule from Lesson 5, the spacing must grow in this order: **between letters < between words < between lines < between paragraphs**, so that proximity groups them correctly.

If leading is used as the basic unit, the spacing between paragraphs and the space above and below headings can be set as multiples of it. For example, if the leading is 24px, set the paragraph spacing at 24px and the space above a heading at 48px. This creates a consistent **vertical rhythm** across the entire page and leads to the baseline grid of the next lesson.

Limits: these numbers are only starting points. The appropriate values change with the font's x-height, the language (Hangul, with its syllable blocks and final consonants, has a different rhythm from Latin script), screen brightness and the reader's eyesight. Rather than fixing a single “correct number,” it is more important to design so that the screen does not break when users change the type size and spacing.

examples.title: Setting the vertical rhythm of body text
body: Condition: body text at 18px, designed with a leading multiplier of 1.5.
Step 1: The height of one line is 18 × 1.5 = 27px.
Step 2: Set the paragraph spacing to 27px, equal to one line height, and the space above a heading to 54px, two line heights.
Interpretation: All vertical spacing becomes a multiple of 27, so lines in several side-by-side columns do not drift out of alignment.

Step 1: 32 × 80 ÷ 1000 = 2.56px is added between the letters.
Step 2: The same +80 on 14px body text adds only 1.12px, but in long sentences it breaks words into scattered clusters and actually makes reading harder.
Interpretation: Tracking has different effects depending on type size and the length of the text, even with the same value. Short capitalized phrases and long body text are treated separately.

design-09.title: Modular Grids and Baseline Grids
explain: The grid in Lesson 3 divided the screen into vertical columns and concentrated on aligning left edges. But a magazine page or the first screen of an app mixes photos, tables, headings and body text, so the **vertical position** must also align for the layout to look orderly. A grid that is also divided into horizontal bands for this purpose is a **modular grid**.

A modular grid is built from three elements.
- **Column**: a vertical division.
- **Row**: a horizontal division.
- **Module**: the single cell formed where a column and a row intersect. An element occupies one module or several.
Modules are separated by a constant **gutter** and surrounded by **margins**. This system was refined in the mid-twentieth century by graphic designers in Switzerland, and Lesson 17 revisits that history.

Column width is determined by calculation. If the page width is $W$, the side margins are $m$, the gutter is $g$ and the number of columns is $n$, then with $n-1$ gutters the width of one column is $$c = \frac{W - 2m - (n-1)g}{n}$$ 이다. 한 요소가 $k$단을 차지하면 그 사이의 거터 $k-1$개도 함께 덮으므로 폭은 $$kc + (k-1)g$$ 가 된다. 예를 들어 $W = 960$, $m = 40$, $g = 20$, $n = 12$이면 $c = (960 - 80 - 220) / 12 = 55$이고, 4단짜리 블록은 $4 \times 55 + 3 \times 20 = 280$이다. (In English: If an element spans k columns, it also covers the k-1 gutters between them, so its width becomes kc + (k-1)g For example, when W = 960, m = 40, g = 20 and n = 12, then c = (960 - 80 - 220) / 12 = 55, and a block four columns wide is 4 \times 55 + 3 \times 20 = 280.)

explain.alt: Modular grid diagram. Inside a white page labeled “페이지 폭 300 · 높이 210” (page width 300, height 210) are grey modules arranged as 3 columns by 3 rows, nine cells in all. Orange block A covers the two left columns of the first row. Below are the labels “사방 여백 20 · 거터 10” (margins of 20 on all sides, gutter 10) and “단 3개 · 줄 3개 (모듈 9칸)” (3 columns, 3 rows, 9 modules).

explain: Read the figure precisely. Subtracting the margins of 20 from the page width of 300 gives a text area of width 260, with two gutters of 10 between the three columns. The module height can be found the same way from the height of 210. Orange block A covers the two columns in the first row together with the gutter between them. The most common mistake when measuring block widths is to forget the gutters.

Vertical alignment follows a **baseline grid**. Horizontal lines are drawn at intervals of the body leading (for example, 24px), and module heights and gutters are set as multiples of the leading. If the module height is 4 lines (96px) and the gutter is 1 line (24px), body text in any column sits on the same heights. The vertical rhythm created in Lesson 8 thus becomes the skeleton of the whole page.

Limits and exceptions: a grid is a basis for judgment, not a rule. Photos that extend past the edge of the text area to the edge of the paper (bleed), or a single element that deliberately breaks out of the grid to draw the eye, read as intentional as long as the grid is clear. On the web, where screen width changes, a single grid cannot be fixed; a 12-column grid on a wide screen is reduced to about 4 columns on a narrow one, so the grid itself changes.

examples.title: Finding block widths on a 12-column grid
body: Condition: width 960px, side margins 40px, gutter 20px, on a 12-column grid, with a body block (8 columns) and a side block (4 columns).
Step 1: The column width is (960 − 80 − 11 × 20) ÷ 12 = 660 ÷ 12 = 55px.

Step 2: The 8-column block is 8 × 55 + 7 × 20 = 580px, and the 4-column block is 4 × 55 + 3 × 20 = 280px. Adding the 20px gutter between the two blocks gives 580 + 20 + 280 = 880px, exactly the width of the text area (960 − 80).
Interpretation: Checking that the sum of block widths and gutters matches the width of the text area catches calculation errors.

examples.title: Setting line height with a baseline grid
body: Condition: body text 16px, leading 24px. Build a 3-row grid with a module height of 4 lines and a gutter of 1 line.
Step 1: The module height is 24 × 4 = 96px, and the gutter is 24px.
Step 2: The height of the 3-row text area is 3 × 96 + 2 × 24 = 336px. This equals 24 × 14, so exactly 14 lines of body text fit.
Interpretation: When the height of the text area is a whole-number multiple of the leading, body text starting from any module sits on the same baseline.

design-10.title: Affordances and Signifiers: From Gibson to Norman
explain: In Lesson 6 you learned that appearance can be a clue to action, the concept of **affordance**. Yet everyone has experienced pulling a door by its bar handle when it was actually a push door. The handle clearly looks graspable, so why was it wrong? To resolve this confusion, you need to know where the word affordance came from and how it changed in design.

The term was coined by the perceptual psychologist **James Gibson**. For Gibson, an affordance is the **action possibility** that an environment offers an animal. It is not a property of the object alone, but a **relationship between the object and the actor**. A flat rock at knee height is a place to sit for an adult, but not for a baby. Moreover, for Gibson an affordance exists whether or not anyone notices it.

The cognitive scientist **Donald Norman** brought this concept into everyday objects and screen design. For designers, what mattered was less whether an action is possible than whether **users notice that possibility**. Norman later separated two concepts clearly. An **affordance** is the action possible in itself, and a **signifier** is a perceivable sign that tells where and how the action should be performed. On screens, any point can be tapped, so most screen problems are problems of signifiers rather than affordances.

Norman also organized other principles that govern the user experience.
- **Mapping**: the spatial correspondence between a control and its result. If the arrangement of burner knobs matches the arrangement of the burners, confusion is avoided.
- **Constraints**: devices that limit the possible actions to prevent mistakes. A charging port that fits in only one direction is an example.
- **Feedback**: immediately telling the user the result of an action (Lesson 6).
- **Conceptual model**: a framework that explains how an object works. It should match the user's expectations (the mental model).
The gap between what the user wants to do and not knowing how to do it is the **gulf of execution**; the gap in interpreting a result that has occurred is the **gulf of evaluation**. Signifiers and mapping narrow the former, and feedback narrows the latter.

Whether an affordance **exists** and whether it is **visible** can be separated into four cases. If it exists and is visible, the design is good. If it exists but is hidden, it is a **hidden affordance** (for example, a menu that appears only on a long press). If it does not exist but appears to, it is a **false affordance** (for example, a decoration that looks like a button but does nothing). If it neither exists nor is visible, there is no problem. When reading examples, it helps to ask these two questions separately.

Limits and issues: many signifiers are not innate but learned **conventions**. That a set of three horizontal lines means a menu, and that blue underlined text is a link, are things people learn. Therefore the same signifier may not work for another culture or generation. There is also a debate: some critics say the flat screen styles that have spread, which remove shadows and borders, blur the distinction between what can be pressed and what cannot; others reply that users have already learned the conventions, so the problem is not serious.

examples.title: A signifier for a door that must be pushed
body: Condition (hypothetical): the entrance doors of a building both have identical bar handles, and a sign reading “미세요” (push) is attached on the outside.
Step 1: A bar handle is read as a signifier for “grasp and pull.” The door must be pushed to open, so the handle's shape conflicts with the actual action.
Step 2: If a flat plate for the palm is placed on the pushing side and a bar handle only on the pulling side, the action becomes evident without a written sign.
Interpretation: The need for written instructions is often itself a sign that the signifier has failed.

examples.title: A card that can be pressed but is not recognized
body: Condition (hypothetical): on an event list screen, tapping a whole card opens its details page, but the card has no border and no arrow.
Step 1: The action of pressing is possible, so the affordance exists. But there is no signal to show it, so it is a hidden affordance.
Step 2: Place an arrow on the right side of the card, and make the background color change when pressed (feedback).
Interpretation: Adding a signifier and feedback together narrowed both the gulf of execution and the gulf of evaluation.

checks.hint: An affordance is a 'possibility'; a signifier is a 'signal'.
checks.explanation: Norman distinguished between the action that is possible (affordance) and the signal that reveals it (signifier).

A perceivable signal that shows where and how to act
The spatial correspondence between a control and its result
Devices that limit possible actions to prevent mistakes

checks.explanation: The square arrangement and the row arrangement do not correspond, so it is impossible to tell which knob controls which burner. This is a mapping problem.

Constraints
Mapping

checks.prompt: In an app's notice, several words are blue and underlined, but tapping them does nothing. What is this case?
checks.hint: Ask separately: is the action possible, or does it only appear to be possible?
checks.explanation: It looks like a link (a learned convention signifier) but cannot actually be pressed, so it is a false affordance.
options: A hidden affordance
A false affordance
A good mapping
A design with no gulf of evaluation

checks.hint: Does Gibson's affordance depend on whether it is perceived?
checks.explanation: For Gibson, an affordance exists as a relationship between actor and environment regardless of perception. Making it noticed is the domain of the signifiers that Norman emphasized.

It exists equally for a child

design-11.title: Fitts's Law: Time to Reach a Target
explain: You know that a “저장” (Save) button placed very small in a corner is inconvenient to press. But to say how much more inconvenient it is, or how much better doubling the button's size would be, requires a model rather than a feeling. The representative model for predicting the time it takes to move a hand or cursor to a target is **Fitts's law**.

The psychologist Paul Fitts ran experiments in the 1950s in which people alternately tapped two targets. The result matched intuition: the targets take longer to reach the **farther** away they are and the **smaller** they are. The key point is that these two act together, as a **ratio of distance to width**, not separately. Doubling the distance while also doubling the width leaves the difficulty almost the same.

The information-theoretic summary of this is the **index of difficulty** $ID$. With distance $D$ and target width $W$, the form widely used in human–computer interaction research today is $$ID = \log_2\left(\frac{D}{W} + 1\right)$$ 이고 단위는 비트다. 이동 시간은 $$MT = a + b \times ID$$ 로 예측한다. $a$와 $b$는 기기와 사람에 따라 실험으로 정하는 상수다. 계산 순서는 ① $D$와 $W$를 잰다 → ② $D/W + 1$을 구한다 → ③ 밑이 2인 로그를 취해 $ID$를 얻는다 → ④ $a + b \times ID$로 시간을 예측한다. (In English: with units in bits. Movement time is predicted as MT = a + b \times ID where a and b are constants determined by experiment for the device and the person. The order of calculation is ① measure D and W → ② compute D/W + 1 → ③ take the base-2 logarithm to obtain ID → ④ predict the time with a + b \times ID.)

explain.alt: Two aiming tasks. Above, a target button A (orange) lies at distance D = 150 from the green start point and has width W = 10. Below, a target button B (orange) lies at distance D = 210 from the green start point and has width W = 70.

explain: Read the figure. For button A, $D = 150$ and $W = 10$, so $150/10 + 1 = 16$ and $\log_2 16 = 4$ bits. Button B is farther away, but with $D = 210$ and $W = 70$, $210/70 + 1 = 4$, which is 2 bits. The farther button B is in fact easier to reach. This shows that judging by distance alone leads to the wrong conclusion.

There are several design implications.
- Make frequently used buttons large and place them close to where the user is.
- On screens used with a mouse, the cursor stops at the edge of the screen, so targets at the edges and corners behave as if they were very wide.
- A menu that opens right where the user pressed reduces the distance to almost zero.
- Conversely, **dangerous, irreversible actions** (for example, deleting everything) should be deliberately placed away from frequently used buttons and protected by a confirmation step so they are hard to press by accident.
The **Hick's law**, which says that the time to choose grows with the number of options, is also used alongside this, but it differs in that it concerns the time spent deciding rather than moving.

Limits: Fitts's law is basically a model of movements that point straight in one direction. On touch screens, a finger does not stop at the edge of the screen the way a cursor does, so the advantage of edges disappears, and the fingertip covers the target, increasing the error for small targets. Areas that a thumb can easily reach when the device is held in one hand must also be considered. In addition, the law does not include the time needed to **find** a target or the time spent **deliberating**.

examples.title: The movement times for the two buttons in the figure
body: Condition: for a certain user and mouse, experiments yielded $a = 200$ms and $b = 100$ms/bit.
Step 1: For button A, $ID = 4$, so $MT = 200 + 100 \times 4 = 600$ms.
Step 2: For button B, $ID = 2$, so $MT = 200 + 100 \times 2 = 400$ms.
Interpretation: The farther button B is 200ms faster. Enlarging a target is often more effective than moving it.

examples.title: Doubling the width
body: Condition: a button with $D = 300$ and $W = 20$ is enlarged to $W = 40$.
Step 1: Originally, $ID = \log_2(15 + 1) = 4$ bits.
Step 2: After enlarging, $ID = \log_2(7.5 + 1) = \log_2 8.5 \approx 3.09$ bits.

Interpretation: Doubling the width does not halve the difficulty; it reduces it by only about 0.9 bits. Because the relationship is logarithmic, the benefit of enlarging a target that is already large becomes progressively smaller.

design-12.title: Mental Models and Accessibility: WCAG Principles and Contrast Ratios
explain: Designers unconsciously picture users similar to themselves: people with good eyesight, two free hands, looking at the screen in a quiet place. But real users include people with weak vision or who listen to the screen with a screen reader, people with an injured arm who use only one hand, and people who view the screen in bright sunlight. Constraints can be permanent, but they can also be temporary or situational. Designing so that the product works under these varied conditions is the job of **accessibility** design.

Lesson 10 said that the **conceptual model** and the user's **mental model** must match for a thing to be easy to use. Accessibility means making sure this model is **conveyed through multiple senses and ways of operating**. If the meaning of a button is conveyed only by color, the model fails to reach users who have trouble distinguishing colors. If the meaning of an image is also conveyed through alternative text, a user who listens to the screen gets the same model.

The **Web Content Accessibility Guidelines** (WCAG), created by the W3C, are organized around four principles.
- **Perceivable**: information must be perceivable through the senses (alternative text, sufficient contrast).
- **Operable**: all functions must be operable (usable by keyboard alone, with enough time).
- **Understandable**: content and operation must be understandable (consistent navigation, error guidance).
- **Robust**: content must be interpretable by a wide range of tools, including assistive technologies (markup that follows standards).
Each criterion is divided into three levels, A, AA and AAA, and AA is commonly the target.

The criterion used most in calculation is the **contrast ratio**. For each color, the **relative luminance** $L$ is found, with black at 0 and white at 1. Let $L_1$ be the brighter color and $L_2$ the darker, then $$CR = \frac{L_1 + 0.05}{L_2 + 0.05}$$ 이다. 흰색과 검정은 $1.05 / 0.05 = 21$로 최댓값 21:1이고, 같은 색끼리는 1:1이다. 0.05를 더하는 것은 화면 주변의 반사광을 반영해 어두운 색 사이의 비율이 무한히 커지지 않게 하기 위해서다. (In English: White against black gives 1.05 / 0.05 = 21, the maximum of 21:1, and a color against itself gives 1:1. The addition of 0.05 reflects ambient light reflected from the screen and keeps the ratio between dark colors from becoming unbounded.)

At level AA, normal body text requires a ratio of **at least 4.5:1**, and large text (about 18pt or more, or about 14pt or more when bold) requires **at least 3:1**. AAA requires 7:1 and 4.5:1 respectively. Elements that are not text, such as the border of a button or the edge of an input field, also require a contrast of at least 3:1 against their surroundings. The latest version (2.2) also sets a minimum size for pressable targets of about 24 × 24 CSS pixels, which connects to Fitts's law in Lesson 11.

Case study (hypothetical): Suppose a fictional shopping app shows errors only with a red border, and uses a grey guidance note (relative luminance 0.30) on a white background. The contrast of the note is $1.05 / 0.35 = 3.0$, which barely clears only the large-text criterion. Because the red border depends on color alone (Lesson 4), it must be accompanied by an icon or by text such as “필수 입력입니다” (This field is required).

Limits: even when every criterion is met, there is no guarantee that a thing is easy to use, so evaluation with real users is necessary. Critics note that the current contrast formula does not adequately reflect differences in font weight and size, and new calculation methods are under discussion. Which countries make accessibility standards a legal obligation is outside the scope of this lesson.

examples.title: Judging a contrast ratio
body: Condition: the text has relative luminance 0.10 and the background 0.70.
Step 1: The background is the lighter one, so $CR = (0.70 + 0.05) / (0.10 + 0.05) = 0.75 / 0.15 = 5.0$.
Step 2: 5.0 exceeds the AA threshold for normal text (4.5) but does not reach AAA (7).
Interpretation: The text can be used at AA level for body text; to meet a higher standard, the text must be made darker.

examples.title: Applying for a course using the keyboard only
body: Condition (hypothetical): Try a local community course registration screen using only the Tab key, without a mouse.
Step 1: When Tab is pressed, the position of focus is lost because no outline shows which element currently has focus (a perceivable and operable problem).
Step 2: Make the focus indicator clear and align the tab order with the screen's reading order.
Interpretation: For keyboard users, the focus indicator is the same as a cursor. The visual hierarchy of Lesson 1 has been applied to the order of focus movement as well.

design-13.title: The Double Diamond and the Human-Centered Design Process
explain: The most common mistake in a meeting about a new service is starting on day one by drawing screen mockups. No matter how good the mockups are, they are useless if they solve the **wrong problem**. Design methodology is a procedure that makes people confirm “what is the problem?” before asking “what should we build?”

The **Double Diamond**, summarized by the British Design Council in the mid-2000s from the working methods of several design firms, draws this process as two diamonds. Each diamond consists of **divergence** (widening thinking) and **convergence** (narrowing it). The first diamond deals with the **problem**, and the second with the **solution**.

The four stages are as follows.
1. **Discover** (diverge): gather broadly, through interviews, observation and research, the situations people actually face.
2. **Define** (converge): group and interpret the collected material, and fix the task to be solved in a single sentence. Questions of the form “How might we ...?” are commonly used.
3. **Develop** (diverge): propose several solutions and quickly test them as prototypes.
4. **Deliver** (converge): refine the remaining proposals after testing, release them and check the reactions.

explain.alt: Two diamonds joined end to end. On the left half of the first diamond is “① 발견” (① Discover); on its right half, “② 정의” (② Define). On the left half of the second diamond is “③ 개발” (③ Develop); on its right half, “④ 전달” (④ Deliver). Above each half are, in order, “확산” (diverge), “수렴” (converge), “확산” (diverge) and “수렴” (converge). Below, the first diamond is labeled “문제 공간” (problem space) and the second “해결 공간” (solution space), and at the bottom it reads “가운데 꼭짓점: 과제 정의서” (center vertex: task definition).

explain: The central vertex where the two diamonds meet is the **task definition**. All activities in the first diamond converge on this single point, and all ideas in the second diamond spread out from it. If the definition is vague, there is no criterion for where the second diamond's ideas should spread. The **affinity diagram**, which groups dozens of notes gathered in the discovery stage by similarity to find themes, is a typical convergent tool of the define stage.

The international standard ISO 9241-210 summarizes a similar idea as **human-centered design**. It runs: understand the context of use → specify user requirements → produce design solutions → evaluate with users; and based on the evaluation results, return to earlier stages and **iterate**. The two models share the starting point of understanding users, and the practice of testing what has been made with users and revising it.

Limits and criticisms: real projects do not pass through the four stages in one go. It is common to realize during development that the problem definition was wrong and to return to the first diamond. Therefore the diagram should be read as a map of a way of thinking rather than a strictly sequential flowchart. There is also criticism that such procedures become empty rituals in which real users are excluded from decisions. In response, **co-design**, which involves users and local residents directly in the design process, has been proposed as an alternative.

examples.title: The library return problem
body: Condition (hypothetical): The usage rate of the return box at a neighborhood library is low.

Step 1 (discover → define): Observing at the entrance for one week showed that about half of first-time visitors could not find the return box and lined up at the information desk. The task was set as “How might we help first-time visitors find the return box within 30 seconds?”

Step 2 (develop → deliver): Three proposals (floor arrows, an entrance sign and moving the return box) were each tested for a day with paper and tape, and the most effective one was installed permanently.
Interpretation: The initial idea of “making the return box more attractive” would likely not have solved the real problem, which was not finding it.

body: Condition (hypothetical): Forty notes were collected from eight interviews.
Step 1: Post the notes on a wall and move similar ones together to form five groups.

Step 2: Title each group in the users' own words, such as “Don't know the opening hours” or “Hard to carry heavy books here,” and choose the group that the most people experienced as the task candidate.
Interpretation: Gathering scattered material into a few themes is convergence in the define stage.

design-14.title: Personas and Customer Journey Maps
explain: A plan to build “an app for every user” sounds good, but in practice it tends to fit no one in particular. When someone says “users will like this” in a design meeting, each team member imagines a different user. Tools that turn research findings into something concrete the whole team can look at together are **personas** and **customer journey maps**.

A **persona** is a **fictional character** constructed to represent behavioral patterns found in research. In software design, Alan Cooper widely popularized this method. The core of a good persona is not demographics such as age or income, but **goals**, **behaviors**, **context of use** and **frustrations**. Choosing one persona from several as the primary persona gives the team a criterion when debating whether to include a feature: “Does the primary persona need this?”

A **customer journey map** lays out, in chronological order, the experience of one persona from first learning about a service to leaving it. Horizontally it lays out the **stages**; vertically, several **layers**.
- **Actions**: what the customer actually does at that stage.
- **Touchpoints**: the media or places where the customer meets the service (app, store, signage).
- **Thoughts and feelings**: the questions the customer holds and the degree of satisfaction or frustration.
- **Opportunities**: ideas for improving the inconveniences.
The emotion layer is often drawn as an **emotion curve** connecting scores. The lowest point on the curve is the **pain point**, and the first candidate for improvement.

explain.alt: Customer journey map for a hypothetical bicycle rental service. Across the top are five stage boxes: “앱 설치” (app installation), “회원 가입” (sign-up), “위치 찾기” (finding a location), “대여” (renting) and “반납” (returning). Below is an emotion axis from −2 to +2 with a line graph. The points for the stages sit at heights +1, −1, 0, +2 and −2 in order. At the bottom is written “감정 점수: 위쪽 만족, 아래쪽 불만 (가상 조사)” (emotion score: upper = satisfaction, lower = dissatisfaction; hypothetical survey).

explain: Read the hypothetical bicycle rental service in the figure. Satisfaction is highest at the renting stage, and the curve drops below the baseline at sign-up and at returning. The return stage is the lowest of all. Still, decisions should not be made on scores alone. Sign-up is experienced only once, but returning is experienced every time the service is used, so the same dissatisfaction improves more experiences when returns are fixed. Scores and frequency must be read together.

A journey map follows one person's experience, so it is strong at revealing inconveniences that no one saw in an organization divided by department. If the app team looked only at the sign-up screen and the field team only at the bike racks, the experience of “returning is inconvenient” as a whole would have been no one's responsibility.

Limits: a persona made at a desk without research evidence merely dresses up the team's preconceptions in a plausible way. Each persona should record which interviews and observations it came from. Also, a person made by averaging several people may in fact be no one, and actual journeys do not run in a single line as a map suggests; they skip ahead and loop back. A map is a tool for conversation, not the facts themselves.

examples.title: Creating one persona card
body: Condition (hypothetical): interviews with twelve bicycle rental users revealed a pattern of “people who commute daily between the subway station and their office.”

Step 1: Create a hypothetical person, “Minseo.” Her goal is to cover the last 1.5 km of her morning commute in ten minutes; her behavior is using the same rental station every morning; her frustration is that the bike racks in front of her office are full during rush hour.
Step 2: Under the persona, record the evidence, for example: “7 of the 12 interviewees mentioned a shortage of return racks.”
Interpretation: A persona with evidence attached lets the team judge the question “Would Minseo use this feature?” by a common standard.

examples.title: Prioritizing pain points
body: Condition: in the journey map in the figure, sign-up scores −1 (happens once in a lifetime) and returning scores −2 (happens at each use).
Step 1: For someone who uses the service twenty times a month, the dissatisfaction with returning repeats twenty times, while the dissatisfaction with sign-up happens just once.
Step 2: Set the return stage as the first improvement task, and then examine the processes behind it using the service blueprint of Lesson 15.
Interpretation: The size of an emotion score and the frequency of an experience must be read together to compare the effects of improvements.

design-15.title: Service Blueprints: Drawing the Invisible Process
explain: A customer journey map is the experience seen through the customer's eyes. But the reasons why returning is inconvenient, or why an ordered bread comes out late, often arise in places the customer cannot see: the work of staff and the internal systems. From a journey map alone, one can learn “where is it inconvenient” but not easily “why is it inconvenient.”

In the 1980s, Lynn Shostack proposed managing a service by drawing it like an architectural blueprint. This is the **service blueprint**. Services are intangible (intangibility), are consumed the moment they are produced (simultaneity), vary in quality with staff and circumstance (heterogeneity), and cannot be stored (perishability). Because of these characteristics, it is necessary to draw the entire process in advance and manage the points where failure occurs.

The blueprint consists of five layers, read from top to bottom, and three lines.
- **Physical evidence**: what the customer sees and touches (screens, signage, packaging).
- **Customer actions**: what the customer does. This is the same as the actions layer of the journey map.
- *Interaction line*: the boundary where the customer and the service meet directly.
- **Front stage**: staff actions carried out in front of the customer.
- *Line of visibility*: below this line, the customer cannot see.
- **Back stage**: staff actions the customer does not see.
- *Internal interaction line*: the boundary where staff meet internal support systems.
- **Support processes**: the systems and other departments' work that underpin the service.

explain.alt: Service blueprint for a hypothetical bakery pickup order. On the left, from top to bottom, the five row labels read “물리적 증거” (physical evidence), “고객 행동” (customer actions), “프론트스테이지” (front stage), “백스테이지” (back stage) and “지원 프로세스” (support processes). The physical evidence row shows the app order screen, a pickup counter sign and a paper bag. The customer actions row shows ordering in the app, arriving at the shop and receiving the bread. The front stage row shows a name check in the middle and handing over the bread on the right. The back stage row shows order confirmation on the left and packaging preparation in the middle. The support processes row shows the order system, inventory management and the payment system. Between the second and third rows is an “interaction line” (상호작용선), between the third and fourth a “line of visibility” (가시선), and between the fourth and fifth an “internal interaction line” (내부 상호작용선), drawn as orange dotted lines.

explain: Read the blueprint in the figure vertically. When the customer arrives at the shop (customer actions), staff check the name (front stage). Below the line of visibility, packaging is prepared (back stage), and this relies on inventory management (support processes). If the customer feels the bread is late, the cause is likely in the layers below rather than in the name check. Following one column from top to bottom to find the cause is the core of reading a blueprint.

The designer marks **failure points** (places where things often go wrong) and **waiting points** (places where customers wait) on the blueprint and revises the processes beneath them. Moving the **line of visibility** is also a design decision. If the kitchen is opened behind glass, cooking, previously back stage, becomes visible to customers, so cleanliness and traffic flow become physical evidence in themselves.

Limits: real services have many cases, so the blueprint easily becomes too large, and a single static drawing cannot capture changes over time or exceptional situations. Also, when focusing only on the customer's experience, it is easy to overlook the burden on back-stage staff. For this reason, it is recommended to draw the blueprint together with staff, and to treat staff experience as a target for improvement as well.

examples.title: Finding the cause of pickup delays
body: Condition (hypothetical): at the bakery in the figure, there are many complaints that “the bread had not been packaged yet when I arrived.”
Step 1: Follow the bread-receiving column from top to bottom. The name check at the front stage is quick, but order confirmation at the back stage happens only when staff look at the screen.
Step 2: Change the support process (the order system) so that new orders are announced with a sound and a light, and set a rule to start packaging ten minutes before the scheduled pickup time.
Interpretation: The cause of the customer's discomfort (waiting) lay below the line of visibility. Decorating the front would not solve it.

examples.title: A decision to move the line of visibility
body: Condition (hypothetical): a noodle shop plans to replace its kitchen wall with glass.
Step 1: Noodle boiling and bowl assembly, which used to be back stage, rise above the line of visibility and take on the character of front stage that customers see.
Step 2: Then the cleanliness of the cooking area, staff hygiene attire and a tidy workstation become new physical evidence and must be designed together.
Interpretation: The position of the line of visibility is not a fixed fact; it is a design variable that changes the service experience.

design-16.title: From the Arts and Crafts Movement to the Bauhaus
explain: When the Industrial Revolution of the nineteenth century let machines produce goods cheaply and quickly, critics complained that products made of poor materials, with handicraft-style ornament stuck on, were flooding the market. What is good design in an age of machine production? The history of modern design can be read as a history of different answers to this question.

In late nineteenth-century Britain, the **Arts and Crafts Movement**, centered on William Morris and others, sought to revive the value of handcraft. It held that good objects come out when the properties of materials are honestly revealed and when the maker takes joy in the work. However, handmade objects were expensive, so the movement ran into a paradox: despite its ideal of good objects for everyone, they were mainly bought by the wealthy.

In early twentieth-century Germany, a different answer emerged. The **Deutscher Werkbund** (German Werkbund), founded in 1907, sought to join artists and industry so that machine production could yield good products. In 1914, a debate within the association pitted Hermann Muthesius, who argued that **standard types** of products should be set for industrial production, against Henry van de Velde, who argued that the individual creativity of artists must be protected. This tension between standardization and individuality recurs in today's discussions of design systems.

The **Bauhaus** was a school founded in Weimar in 1919 by the architect Walter Gropius. It moved to Dessau in 1925 and to Berlin in 1932, and closed in 1933 under pressure from the Nazi regime. Students first went through a **preliminary course** exploring materials, form and color, and then learned in **workshops** such as metal, furniture, weaving and printing. In the early years, handcraft and expressionist use of color were strong, but from the mid-1920s the school turned toward prototypes for industrial production under the slogan “Art and Technology, a New Unity.”

The term **functionalism** is often used to link the Bauhaus and modern design. The phrase “form follows function,” written by the American architect Louis Sullivan, came to symbolize this attitude. Ornament was removed, geometric forms and primary colors were used, and workshops produced experiments such as furniture from bent steel tubes and typefaces that used only lowercase letters without capitals. Many of the principles of point, line and plane, grid and hierarchy from the first stage of this course were organized into the curriculum in this period.

Case study (hypothetical): Compare two teapots. Teapot A has a flower-pattern relief over its entire body and a thin, curved handle. Teapot B has a plain cylindrical body without decoration, a thick handle attached toward the back of the center of gravity, and a vent hole in the lid. A functionalist reading holds that B's form derives from the functions of holding, pouring and washing. However, it can be argued that the pleasure or cultural meaning that decoration gives the user is also a kind of function.

Limits and issues: the Bauhaus existed only briefly, but some assessments say it has since been inflated into a myth. There are criticisms that the “universal” good form that functionalism advocated was in fact the particular taste of the European middle class. Also, though it was a school of equality, female students were mostly assigned to the weaving workshop, a point now being re-examined. Historical movements should be read not as hero stories but together with the problems and limits of their time.

examples.title: Calculating periods from a timeline
body: Condition: The Bauhaus opened in 1919, moved to Dessau in 1925, moved to Berlin in 1932 and closed in 1933.

Interpretation: The Dessau period, when workshop production and prototype design for industry were active, occupies the center of the school's history.

Step 2: The Bauhaus, in its later years, accepted machine production and tried to design simple prototypes suited to it.
Interpretation: The two movements share honest materials and criticism of ornament, but their attitudes toward machines are opposite.

design-17.title: The Swiss International Style and Postmodern Design
explain: After World War II, international trade, multinational companies and international events grew, creating a need for a visual language that people of different languages and cultures could read quickly and clearly. The **international typographic style** refined in Basel and Zurich in the 1950s, often called the **Swiss style**, was a representative answer to this demand.

The Swiss style has the following characteristics.
- Positions every element according to a **modular grid** (Lesson 9).
- Uses **sans-serif** typefaces without decoration. Helvetica and Univers, which appeared around 1957, spread widely with this movement.
- Aligns text to the left, leaves the right edge naturally uneven, and creates tension through an **asymmetrical** composition.
- Puts **objective photographs** and information itself first, rather than illustration.
Designers such as Josef Müller-Brockmann regarded the designer's responsibility as conveying information in an orderly way rather than expressing personal taste.

The style spread widely as a **corporate visual identity** system. Guidelines defining logos, typefaces, colors and grids were created so that branches around the world communicated with the same appearance. Today's design systems and design tokens inherit the same idea: fixing rules in advance to maintain consistency.

From the 1960s on, a backlash arose. Responding to “less is more,” an idea attributed to the architect Mies van der Rohe, Robert Venturi countered with “less is a bore,” defending complexity, contradiction and historical quotation. The **Memphis Group**, formed in Milan in 1981 around Ettore Sottsass, mocked the solemnity of functionalism with intense primary colors, playful patterns and furniture whose forms twisted utility. In graphic design, Wolfgang Weingart and others, who taught in Basel, deliberately disrupted grids and overlapped letters; as personal computers spread in the 1980s and 1990s, work that freely stacked and deconstructed letters increased. These currents are grouped together as **postmodern design**.

Case study (hypothetical): Consider two posters for the same “City Music Festival.” Poster 1 has a four-column grid on a white background, a left-aligned sans-serif title, and the date and place organized in a uniform size system at the bottom. Poster 2 has tilted, overlapping letters on a fluorescent pink and yellow background, with photo fragments scattered without a grid. Poster 1 follows the clarity of the Swiss style, and poster 2 the expressiveness and layered meaning of postmodernism. Which one is “right” depends on the nature of the event, the audience and the amount of information to convey.

Issues: the Swiss style regarded sans-serif and grids as **neutral**, but critics say that even this “neutrality” is the product of a particular era, region and corporate culture. Conversely, postmodern experiments widened the range of expression but are said to risk sacrificing legibility and accessibility (Lesson 12). Today's design largely takes a mixed path rather than choosing one: information is organized into a clear system, while expression is added as the context suits.

examples.title: The same festival, two approaches
body: Condition (hypothetical): Create a poster for the “Children's Invention Contest” at a city science museum.
Step 1 (Swiss approach): Arrange the title, schedule and application method on a four-column grid in a clear hierarchy, using just one sans-serif. Information is easy to find quickly.

Step 2 (postmodern approach): Tilt a handwriting-like title and overlay drawings of inventions. This preserves atmosphere, but the application method is separated into a distinct, clear box to keep it legible.
Interpretation: The two approaches are not opposing right answers; they are choices about what to prioritize for the same task.

examples.title: A visual identity guideline
body: Condition (hypothetical): The fictional airline “Bluebird Air” wants to unify the signage at thirty locations around the world.
Step 1: The guideline sets the clear space around the logo, two typefaces, three colors and a 12-column grid.
Step 2: Each location's designers produce their signage by changing only the content within the guideline.
Interpretation: This shows why the Swiss style spread as corporate identity: the power of consistency through rules.

design-18.title: Sustainable Eco-Design: Life-Cycle Thinking and Circular Design
explain: Even an attractive, easy-to-use product consumes resources, is moved, used and discarded, and places a burden on the environment at each step. Many design teams first reduce packaging for the sake of sustainability, yet for a product that uses electricity, most of the impact may come from the use stage. To know where a change would have the greatest effect, you must look at the whole life of the product in numbers.

**Life cycle assessment** (LCA) is a method of dividing a product's life into stages and adding up the environmental impacts of each. The stages are generally **raw material extraction → manufacturing → transport → use → disposal** (end of life). International standards (ISO 14040 and 14044) specify the procedure, and a **functional unit** (for example, “boiling one liter of water 1,000 times”), the basis for comparison, must be set first so that different products can be compared fairly.

The share of each stage is found by simple proportion. If the emissions of stage $i$ are $E_i$, its share is $$p_i = \frac{E_i}{\sum_j E_j} \times 100$$ (%)이다. 비중이 큰 단계를 고치는 것이 같은 노력으로 더 큰 효과를 낸다. 한 단계를 $x$만큼 줄이면 전체는 $E_i \times x$만큼 줄어든다. (In English: (%). Improving the stage with the largest share yields a bigger effect for the same effort. If a stage is reduced by x, the total decreases by E_i \times x.)

explain.alt: Horizontal bar chart titled “가상의 전기 주전자 한 대의 수명주기 배출량” (lifecycle emissions of one hypothetical electric kettle). Raw material extraction 4, manufacturing 2, transport 1, use 12, disposal 1; only the use bar is orange. Below it reads “단위: kg CO2e (가상 값)” (unit: kg CO2e; hypothetical values).

explain: Read the hypothetical electric kettle in the figure. The total is 4 + 2 + 1 + 12 + 1 = 20 kg CO2e, and the use stage is the largest. Halving the transport emissions by lightening the packaging reduces the total by only 0.5, but raising thermal performance to cut the use stage by 20% reduces it by 2.4. For this product, **design for the use stage**, such as insulation and displaying the amount of water, comes first. Conversely, for an unpowered chair or garment, raw materials and manufacturing may be larger, so the conclusion differs by product.

The principles of circular design are as follows.
- **Reduce**: cut the use of materials and energy.
- **Long life and repair**: assemble with screws so that parts can be replaced, and make forms that do not tire.
- **Design for disassembly**: use a single material, or make separation by material easy.
- **Reuse and recycling**: make the product a resource again after its life ends.
McDonough and Braungart proposed “cradle to cradle,” with **biological cycles**, in which materials return safely to nature, and **technical cycles**, in which materials keep circulating within industry, in place of a straight line of use and discard. Dieter Rams's phrase “Less, but better” points in the same direction.

Limits and issues: LCA results vary greatly depending on the data used and where the boundary is drawn. There is a **rebound effect**, in which, after efficiency is raised, the product is used more often and in greater amounts, so the savings shrink. Recycling often turns materials into lower-quality ones, a process called downcycling. Moreover, **greenwashing**, which inflates a small improvement to suggest that the whole product is environmentally friendly, misleads consumers. Designers must disclose the basis and boundaries of their figures and claim only as much as they have actually improved.

examples.title: Comparing the effects of two improvements
body: Condition: The kettle in the figure (total 20 kg CO2e) has two proposed improvements. Option 1 lightens the packaging, reducing transport from 1 to 0.5. Option 2 strengthens insulation, reducing use from 12 to 9.6 (a 20% cut).
Step 1: After option 1, the total is 19.5, a reduction of 2.5%.
Step 2: After option 2, the total is 17.6, a reduction of 12%.
Interpretation: The use stage accounts for 60% of the total, so improving that stage is far more effective than an equal percentage improvement elsewhere.

examples.title: The effect of extending lifetime
body: Condition: Convert the emissions outside the use stage of the same kettle (raw materials 4 + manufacturing 2 + transport 1 + disposal 1 = 8) into a yearly figure over a five-year lifetime.
Step 1: With a five-year life, the annual burden is 8 ÷ 5 = 1.6.
Step 2: If a structure that allows easy part replacement extends the life to ten years, the annual burden falls to 0.8, half as much.
Interpretation: Designs that encourage long use and repair reduce the burden of the non-use stages by spreading it over time.

design-19.title: Integrated Problem Solving: Redesigning the Return Experience of a Public Bike App
explain: The tools learned so far are most powerful not when used separately but when they work together on a single problem. This lesson is a practice in which one task, redesigning a hypothetical public bike app called “Blue Wheel” (푸른바퀴), is handled by cross-referencing everything from research to screen design to environmental impact.

Situation (hypothetical): As seen in the customer journey map in Lesson 14, the emotion score of the return stage is the lowest. In interviews, the phrases “If the racks are full, I don't know where to go” and “I'm not sure whether the return actually registered” came up repeatedly. The redesign proceeds along the double diamond (Lesson 13).

The flow of analysis is as follows.
1. **Defining the problem**: use the journey map (Lesson 14) to select the pain point, and set priorities by considering frequency and scores together.
2. **Tracing the cause**: follow the return column of the service blueprint (Lesson 15) from top to bottom to examine the back-stage and support processes, such as updating the rack status and the relocation truck.
3. **Screen design**: lay out the return screen with the grid (Lesson 9), and use the typographic hierarchy (Lessons 7 and 8) so that “the nearest empty rack” is read first.
4. **Interaction and accessibility**: check the size and placement of the return confirmation button with Fitts's law (Lesson 11), and the contrast of text and buttons with WCAG (Lesson 12). Signal completion of the return with clear feedback (Lessons 6 and 10).
5. **Sustainability**: consider the environmental burden of service operations as well, such as the relocation truck's trips, using the life-cycle perspective (Lesson 18).

explain.alt: Customer journey map of a hypothetical bicycle rental service. Five stage boxes across the top read “앱 설치” (app installation), “회원 가입” (sign-up), “위치 찾기” (finding a location), “대여” (renting) and “반납” (returning). Below is an emotion axis from −2 to +2 with a line graph. The points for the stages sit at heights +1, −1, 0, +2 and −2 in order. At the bottom is written “감정 점수: 위쪽 만족, 아래쪽 불만 (가상 조사)” (emotion score: upper = satisfaction, lower = dissatisfaction; hypothetical survey).

explain: Reading the figure again, the first target for the redesign is the return stage. But changing only the screen leaves the cause of “the racks are full” intact. Viewed through the blueprint, the cause may lie in a support process that does not update rack status in real time, and in a slow back-stage relocation. The screen design plays the role of honestly showing this information, and it must be paired with operational improvement.

Limits of integrated judgment: the conclusions of the individual tools may conflict. For example, enlarging the return button is good according to Fitts's law, but on a small screen it shrinks the area of the map. Increasing relocation trucks improves the return experience but raises transport emissions. Such conflicts cannot be solved by a single formula; placing the evidence side by side and making the priorities explicit is the judgment expected at the undergraduate level.

examples.title: The grid and the button on the return screen
body: Condition: a 360px wide screen, side margins of 16px, gutters of 16px, a four-column grid, with the return confirmation button spanning two columns.
Step 1: The column width is (360 − 32 − 3 × 16) ÷ 4 = 280 ÷ 4 = 70px. The two-column button is 2 × 70 + 16 = 156px.

Step 2: With the button height set to 50px, if the thumb travels 150px vertically from the top of the screen to the button's center (the width in the direction of movement is the button height), then $ID = \log_2(150/50 + 1) = 2$ bits, a relatively low difficulty.
Interpretation: The grid calculation determines the button size, and that size in turn determines the difficulty of operation. Tools from two lessons connect within a single decision.

examples.title: Checking the contrast of the return-complete feedback
body: Condition: “Return complete” (반납 완료) is shown in white text (1.0) on a green background with relative luminance 0.20.

Step 2: This falls short of the AA threshold of 4.5 for normal text, so either darken the background, or enlarge the text to meet the large-text threshold, and add a check mark icon so that color is not relied on alone.
Interpretation: It is not enough for feedback to merely exist; everyone must be able to perceive it.

design-20.title: Capstone: Integrated Design Proposal
explain: The task of the final lesson is to write an **integrated design proposal** for a hypothetical service of your own choosing. Since this department does not upload works or grade them as good or bad, the deliverable is not a picture but a **written account of design judgments and their grounds**. A good proposal consistently explains “why it was decided this way,” rather than offering flashy mockups.

The proposal is written in the following eight-part frame.
1. **Task definition**: the target service and a task sentence of the form “How might we ...?” (Lesson 13).
2. **Research plan and personas**: whom to meet and by what method, and the primary persona with its evidence (Lesson 14).
3. **Journey map**: stages, emotion curve, pain points and their frequency (Lesson 14).
4. **Service blueprint**: an analysis of the cause, following the column of the largest pain point down past the line of visibility (Lesson 15).
5. **Screen system**: numbers such as grid calculations, typographic hierarchy and leading (Lessons 7–9).
6. **Interaction and accessibility**: the Fitts's-law difficulty of key buttons, contrast ratios, and checks of keyboard use and alternative text (Lessons 10–12).
7. **Sustainability**: the life-cycle share and improvement direction of products or operations related to the service (Lesson 18).
8. **Evaluation plan and limits**: how success will be confirmed, and what this proposal does not cover.

The eight parts must connect with one another. The pain point chosen in the task definition must be the lowest point of the journey map; the blueprint explains its cause; the screen and operational improvements target that cause; and the evaluation metrics must measure that same inconvenience again. If even one part points to a different target, the proposal becomes a patchwork of plausible pieces.

Historical perspectives (Lessons 16 and 17) can also serve as grounds for judgment. For an information-heavy screen, the clear grid of the Swiss style may be the reference, while for a cover that must express a brand's character, the expressiveness of postmodernism may be. Stating which tradition was followed, and why it suits this task, turns a design decision from a matter of taste into an argument.

Self-criticism is half of the capstone. After writing, check one by one: “Is there any sentence asserted without evidence?”, “Do the numbers agree with each other (does the sum of block widths equal the width of the text area)?”, “Is there any information that relies only on color?”, and “Did I inflate the environmental improvement?” This lesson's task is not graded, so use the checklist as your own reviewer.

examples.title: An example outline for a proposal
body: Condition (hypothetical): redesign the reservation and return experience of a neighborhood “shared tool lending station.”

Step 1: The task definition is “How might a first-time resident borrow the tool they need within five minutes, without worrying about the state of the tool when they return it?” The primary persona is a resident who has just moved and is assembling furniture, and the evidence is an interview with ten users.

Step 2: The lowest point of the journey map was “checking for damage at return,” and the blueprint showed that the inspection standards differed from staff member to staff member. The proposed improvements are to show the inspection items on screen with photos, and to standardize the staff inspection checklist.
Interpretation: Because the screen improvement (front stage) and the operational improvement (back stage) target the same pain point, the proposal is consistent.

examples.title: Correcting a draft through self-critique
body: Condition: In the screen system section of the draft outline above, it was written “4-column grid, column width 80px.” The screen width is 360px, with margins of 16px and gutters of 16px.
Step 1: Recalculating gives (360 − 32 − 48) ÷ 4 = 70px. The 80px figure forgot the margins or the gutters.
Step 2: Correct the figure to 70px and update the two-column button width of 156px as well.
Interpretation: Checking the consistency between numbers is the surest way to catch hidden errors in a proposal that looks plausible on the surface.
